-1.1 Fix a bounded Lipschitz function $f:Z\to\mathbb R$. Convolve it in the periodic position variables and Euclidean velocity variables with a nonnegative smooth approximate identity of radius $\epsilon$; call the result $f_\epsilon$. Differentiating the compactly supported smooth kernel under the integral shows $f_\epsilon$ is smooth and bounded by $\|f\|_\infty$. Since the kernel moves position by at most $\epsilon$ and velocity by at most $\epsilon$, the sum metric gives $\|f_\epsilon-f\|_\infty\le2\epsilon\operatorname{Lip}(f)$. +1.1 Fix a bounded Lipschitz function $f:Z\to\mathbb R$. For $0<\epsilon<1/4$, define $\eta_\epsilon^{\mathbb R}(v)=\epsilon^{-d}\eta(v/\epsilon)$ and periodize it to $\mathbb T^d$ by $\eta_\epsilon^{\mathbb T}(x)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z^d}\epsilon^{-d}\eta((\widetilde x+n)/\epsilon)$, where $\widetilde x$ is any representative; the sum is finite locally, independent of the representative, has integral one against normalized Haar measure, and is supported where $d_{\mathbb T^d}(x,0)\le\epsilon$. Set $f_\epsilon(x,v)=\int_{\mathbb T^d}\int_{\mathbb R^d}\eta_\epsilon^{\mathbb T}(x-y)\eta_\epsilon^{\mathbb R}(v-w)f(y,w)\,dw\,dy$. Differentiating the compactly supported smooth kernels under the integral shows that $f_\epsilon$ is smooth, and their nonnegativity and unit integrals give $\|f_\epsilon\|_\infty\le\|f\|_\infty$. On their support, $d_{\mathbb T^d}(x,y)\le\epsilon$ and $|v-w|\le\epsilon$, so $\|f_\epsilon-f\|_\infty\le2\epsilon\operatorname{Lip}(f)$. For each $R>0$, $\chi_R(v)f_\epsilon(x,v)$ is in $C_c^\infty(Z)$, so its integrals agree by the hypothesis. Let $R\to\infty$ and apply [F3] to each probability measure; then let $\epsilon\downarrow0$ and use uniform convergence. Thus $\mu$ and $\nu$ have equal integrals for every bounded Lipschitz $f$. Hence $h_n(z)=\max(0,1-n d_Z(z,C))$ is bounded Lipschitz and decreases pointwise to $\mathbf1_C$. Step 1.1 gives equal integrals of $h_n$, and [F3] gives $\mu(C)=\nu(C)$. The empty closed set has mass zero for both. Let $\mathcal D:=\{E\in\mathcal B(Z):\mu(E)=\nu(E)\}$. Since $\mu$ and $\nu$ are probabilities, $Z\in\mathcal D$; equality of total mass makes $\mathcal D$ closed under complements in $Z$, and countable additivity makes it closed under countable disjoint unions. Thus $\mathcal D$ is a lambda-system. The $d_Z$ sum metric induces the product topology on $Z$, so its closed sets form a pi-system containing $Z$ and generating $\mathcal B(Z)$. Apply [F4] to this pi-system and $\mathcal D$ to get $\mu=\nu$. [F1, F3, F4, step 1.1] ∎

Applying the identity to $g(x,v)=\chi_R(v)$ gives integrals that increase to $\int_Z\rho_s\,dx\,dv$ by [F6]. Apply [F7] to conclude $\rho_s\,dx\,dv=\mu_s$, so $\rho_s$ is the density of $\mu_s$. [F3, F4, F5, F6, F7, F8, step 5.1, construct, algebra]

Define $D_x(s)=\int d_{\mathbb T^d}(X_s,Y_s)\,d\pi_0$, $D_v(s)=\int|V_s-W_s|\,d\pi_0$, and $D=D_x+D_v$. The torus distance along absolutely continuous curves has upper derivative at most $|V_s-W_s|$. Writing both accelerations as integrals against the same $\pi_0$, the force difference is bounded by $A(d_{\mathbb T^d}(X_s,Y_s)+D_x(s))$. On every bounded time slab the velocity difference is bounded by its integrable initial difference plus $2\|k\|_\infty |s|$, and the acceleration difference is at most $2\|k\|_\infty$. Integrate the pathwise distance inequalities in time and against $\pi_0$; Tonelli [F6] justifies the order of integration and gives $D(s)\le D(0)+\int_0^s(D_v(r)+2A D_x(r))\,dr\le D(0)+(1+2A)\int_0^sD(r)\,dr$. Gronwall [F9] gives $D(s)\le e^{(1+2A)s}D(0)$. For negative time, the transformation $R(x,v)=(x,-v)$ sends a solution run backward to a forward solution starting from $R_\#\mu_0$ (and likewise for $\nu_0$). Explicitly, if the original characteristic starts at $(x,v)$ with law $\mu_0$, set $\widetilde X_r=X_{-r}(x,v)$ and $\widetilde V_r=-V_{-r}(x,v)$; the reversed initial state is $(x,-v)$. Then $\dot{\widetilde X}=\widetilde V$ and $\dot{\widetilde V}=F_{\mu_{-r}}(\widetilde X)=F_{R_\#\mu_{-r}}(\widetilde X)$, because the force depends only on position. Thus $R_\#\mu_{-r}$ is a forward solution starting at $R_\#\mu_0$. Since $R$ preserves $d_Z$, the positive-time estimate for these reversed solutions proves the estimate with $|s|$. [F1, F4, F6, F9, given, construct]
